reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: Most life-threatening reactions are IgE-mediated and begin within minutes to a couple of hours of ingestion, with skin, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and cardiovascular signs in varying combinations
A short list of foods accounts for the majority of reactions: cow's milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, wheat, soy, fish, and shellfish, with peanut and tree nut allergy tending to persist into adult life

Diagnosis rests on a careful history correlating a specific food with reproducible symptoms, supported by skin prick testing or serum specific IgE, with the oral food challenge remaining the reference standard
A positive skin or blood test signals sensitisation but does not by itself confirm clinical allergy, so results must be interpreted against the history to avoid needless dietary restriction
Pollen-food (oral allergy) syndrome causes localised oral itching from raw fruits and vegetables that cross-react with pollens and is usually mild because the allergens are heat-labile

Cornerstones of management are strict avoidance of the culprit food, patient education on label reading and hidden exposures, and a written emergency action plan with a self-injectable adrenaline device
Adrenaline given intramuscularly is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and must never delay adrenaline
Cofactors such as exercise, alcohol, NSAIDs, and intercurrent infection can lower the reaction threshold, as in food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis
Early rather than delayed introduction of allergenic foods such as peanut in infancy reduces the risk of developing allergy in high-risk children
reference.pathophysiology: IgE-mediated food allergy arises when sensitisation to dietary protein leads to allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure the allergen cross-links surface IgE, triggering degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, and mucus secretion. Non-IgE and mixed mechanisms (e.g. eosinophil- and T-cell-driven) underlie disorders such as eosinophilic oesophagitis and food protein-induced enterocolitis, which produce more delayed, predominantly gastrointestinal disease. Loss of oral tolerance, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and cutaneous sensitisation (notably through eczematous skin) are contributing factors.
additionalDifferentials: Food intolerance (e.g. lactase deficiency) without immune mechanism
Scombroid (histamine) poisoning and other food toxin reactions
Eosinophilic oesophagitis and other eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders
Carbohydrate (alpha-gal) allergy causing delayed reactions to mammalian meat
Panic or vasovagal episodes mimicking systemic reactions
additionalInvestigations: Skin prick testing to suspected foods interpreted alongside the clinical history
Serum allergen-specific IgE, including component-resolved testing where available
Supervised oral food challenge as the definitive diagnostic test
Serum tryptase during and after a suspected anaphylactic event
Elimination-and-reintroduction dietary trials for suspected non-IgE disease
redFlags: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise, stridor, wheeze, hypotension, or collapse requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline
Rapidly progressive symptoms after a known trigger, especially in patients with asthma who are at higher risk of fatal reactions
Biphasic reaction recurring hours after apparent recovery
Repeated accidental exposures or reactions despite avoidance suggesting inadequate education or hidden allergens
reference.prognosis: Milk, egg, wheat, and soy allergy commonly resolve during childhood, whereas peanut, tree nut, fish, and shellfish allergy usually persist for life. With reliable avoidance and prompt access to adrenaline, most patients do well, but unrecognised or undertreated anaphylaxis can be fatal.
pitfalls: Diagnosing allergy from a positive test alone without a supporting history, leading to unnecessary and potentially harmful dietary elimination
Relying on antihistamines or steroids for anaphylaxis instead of giving adrenaline promptly
Failing to prescribe, or not teaching correct use of, a self-injectable adrenaline device
Overlooking cofactors and hidden or cross-contaminating allergens in processed foods and restaurant meals
management: Strict avoidance of the culprit food, with structured education on label reading, cross-contamination and hidden exposures
Provide a written emergency anaphylaxis action plan and prescribe self-injectable adrenaline auto-injectors, with training for the patient and carers
Treat mild reactions with oral antihistamines, reserving adrenaline as first-line for any features of anaphylaxis
Consider allergen-specific oral immunotherapy (desensitisation), for example to peanut, within a specialist service
Optimise coexisting atopic conditions such as eczema and asthma, since poorly controlled asthma worsens anaphylaxis risk
Involve a dietitian to ensure nutritional adequacy and avoid unnecessary dietary restriction, particularly in children
Arrange specialist allergy follow-up with periodic reassessment and supervised oral food challenges, since milk, egg, wheat and soy allergy often resolve in childhood
